Title: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/openai-to-acquire-pierre

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/openai-to-acquire-pierre/

Markdown Content:
Today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire [Pierre Computer Company, Inc⁠(opens in a new window)](https://pierre.computer/). (“Pierre”), the company behind [Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window)](https://code.storage/) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re [scaling Git at OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/scaling-git-at-openai/) with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

## Craftsmanship meets scale for the agentic era

We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.

That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ _Edit_ mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released _Highlights_, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

## Bringing the work together in Codex

Pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

_The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies._

Title: Daybreak Red is now available in AWS GovCloud (US-East)

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/daybreak-red-aws-govcloud

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/daybreak-red-aws-govcloud/

Markdown Content:
Building on the availability of Daybreak models on Amazon Bedrock, GPT‑5.6 Cyber is now available to approved customers [in AWS GovCloud (US-East)⁠(opens in a new window)](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/openai-daybreak-red-govcloud-east/) through Daybreak Red. This expansion gives government security teams a new way to apply advanced cybersecurity capabilities within the AWS environments they use to support critical missions.

Daybreak Red provides access to OpenAI’s purpose-trained cybersecurity models for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing. GPT‑5.6 Cyber can help defenders investigate complex software weaknesses, reproduce vulnerabilities in controlled settings, and develop mitigations. Qualified security practitioners should review findings and proposed fixes before implementation.

## Bringing frontier cybersecurity capabilities to government teams

For government organizations, adopting advanced cybersecurity capabilities requires more than model performance. Teams also need to work within established security, governance, and operational requirements.

Availability in AWS GovCloud (US-East) gives eligible teams a path to incorporate GPT‑5.6 Cyber into those workflows through Amazon Bedrock. Defenders can use it to reason through security findings, assess their impact, and evaluate fixes, helping connect vulnerability research to practical improvements in defense.

Daybreak Red gives verified defenders greater latitude for authorized cybersecurity work, with fewer refusals for these tasks alongside stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls.

For Daybreak Red on Amazon Bedrock, inference data is not used to train models, and customers do not need to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI.

## Get started

Access requires OpenAI Daybreak Red approval and AWS provisioning. To get started, complete the [Daybreak application](https://openai.com/form/enterprise-trusted-access-for-cyber/) or contact your OpenAI or AWS account team about eligibility. Once approved, work with your AWS account team to enable access. Daybreak Red approval does not automatically enable model access on AWS.

Title: A thousand fewer paths to root

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/

Markdown Content:
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.

Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.

We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.

In June, as part of our [Patch the Planet initiative](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/), we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.

## Why the Linux kernel

The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.

The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.

## Cost analysis

The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.

Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.

## The vulnerability research pipeline

Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:

*   **Vulnerability discovery:** Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.

*   **Dynamic validation:** Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.

*   **Exploitability assessment:** Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.

*   **Patch generation**: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.

*   **Human review**: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.

At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

### Vulnerability discovery

Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.

#### Scout agents

Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.

This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.

Animation showing scout agents exploring Linux kernel code areas and audit targets.

#### Analyst agents

Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the [Codex Security plugin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/plugins/tree/main/plugins/codex-security). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.

Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.

### Vulnerability validation

A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.

We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.

For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.

Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.

Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.

The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.

### Exploitability assessment

Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.

An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.

Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.

The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.

We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.

The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.

On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.

### Patch generation

For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.

Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with [Patch the Planet](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) commitment to support open-source projects.

## Findings

In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.

### Maintainers are moving quickly to patch vulnerabilities

During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.

articles.content:
The November 3 midterm results gave Democrats full control of Congress, setting the stage for what could be one of the most divided U.S. governments this decade, with Republicans in the White House.
Tuesday’s results suggest that anger over data centers, the large facilities that house the computers powering AI, is becoming a political force. With Democrats now in control of Congress, that could lead to new limits on where data centers can be built and how much say local communities have.
Data centers became a ballot-box issue in various states. An
NBC exit poll
showed how concerned voters are about AI: More than half of respondents believe that AI will do more harm than good, while almost 80% are against the building of data centers in their neighborhoods. Almost 60%, meanwhile, said data centers were a
crucial or major factor
in their vote. Nadine Smith, president and CEO of the racial justice organization Color of Change, called Tuesday’s election a referendum on “who this economy is built for.”
“National security matters,” Smith said, referring to a common argument from data center supporters that the infrastructure is essential for the U.S. to stay ahead in war and in its rivalry with China. “And so do the families in South Memphis breathing exhaust from the gas turbines powering an AI supercomputer.” (She was referring to xAI’s data center in Memphis, Tennessee, which uses gas turbines for power.)
Voters in several states pushed back against the AI buildout, even as pro-AI super PACs spent millions hoping to sway them this midterm. The anti-data center backlash was especially felt in states like Ohio, where OpenAI has eyed a $500 billion data center, backed by more than $100 billion in financing from Nvidia. In fact,
the Ohio county
where Meta had planned a 700,000-square-foot facility just passed a ban on data centers, and local communities across the state overwhelmingly voted against data center buildout measures.
Analysts at
Morgan Stanley predict that
Democratic governor-elect Amy Acton will also pose a major risk to Ohio’s data center buildout. Elsewhere, candidates in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Georgia, and South Carolina all won seats after taking a stance against the rapid buildout of data centers. “It is clear that money does not buy outcomes,” said Anshi Bhatt, a tech and policy researcher, adding that in modern politics, creating a “local villain” is one way to build campaign momentum.
Likely next steps include more construction moratoriums or requiring data centers to pay for their own power grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to nearby communities. Goldman Sachs, in fact, predicts data center construction delays in states like Georgia and Texas because of Democratic gains.
Democratic control of Congress could also improve the odds for bills like the one Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced earlier this year, though any such bill would also face a possible veto. It proposes a nationwide moratorium on new data centers until Congress adds new guardrails and ensures that the buildout does not raise electricity costs, harm the environment, or proceed without community approval.
There are also bills like the GRID Savings Act, proposed by New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, which would prevent grid infrastructure costs from being passed on to communities during large AI data center buildouts.
The environment is also a major concern, especially at xAI’s data center in Memphis and at the data centers throughout Virginia, known as the world capital of data centers, where gas turbines are used for power. Maia Woluchem, program director at Data & Society, a nonprofit research group, believes that changes to energy regulations, land rights, and other environmental policies could affect the data center buildout, especially as congressional Democrats look further into the Trump administration’s rollback of certain energy protections,
as the New York Times reported they might
.
“Regardless of federal action, I could imagine that we will see additional movement at the state and local level, given the momentum that’s been building from the ground up,” Woluchem continued, citing governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who supports a statewide moratorium on data centers, as an example. Both Hinojosa and Gov. Greg Abbott called for some limits, but Hinojosa centered much of her campaign on opposing data centers, a notable choice in Texas, whose electrical grid has proved vulnerable over the past decade.
But the hard part is still to come. Smith, for example, is now expecting a fight, or even more executive orders, to bypass what Congress is now likely to block. “Even among Democrats, a blanket freeze is contested,” she said, referring to some Democrats’ worry that a moratorium could slow AI progress and hurt national security.
She also expects AI lobbyists to start calling lawmakers. “Democrats ran on making Big Tech pay,” Smith said. “Our job is to make sure they remember it once the cameras leave.”
The backlash runs deeper than the buildings themselves, which aren’t new. One private equity executive told me recently that people don’t necessarily hate data centers, but rather AI, and that data centers have become a stand-in for people’s fears and anxieties about the technology. “It does look like the results are pointing to a real frustration with tech power at minimum,” Woluchem said, noting that this is also a bipartisan issue.
For the past month, people have told me they are worried about data centers’ effect on the environment and about their
lack of say
in whether they’re built.
Amazon, for example, built a data center in Gilroy, California,
without many residents knowing
, by satisfying a 45-year-old zoning law. Vague or outdated zoning laws, along with requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) barring them from discussing data center projects, have only fueled people’s outrage about the buildout. Data centers have also received billions in tax breaks, and although many tech companies have touted the benefits, such as
jobs
and community programs, for many people, that simply wasn’t enough.
People want to know they still have a say in what happens in their communities. Many also fear that AI buildouts will mainly enrich a few wealthy people while their communities suffer and living costs rise.
“If AI infrastructure is truly a national priority, then the companies building it can afford to pay for their own power, meet clean air standards, disclose what they use, and build with the consent of the people who live next door,” Smith said. “Families should never be subsidizing the richest corporations in history through their utility bills.”

articles.summary: AI industry PACs spent millions influencing the 2026 midterms, with mixed results. Political groups are already looking toward the next election cycle.
articles.summary_ko: AI 산업을 지지하고 반대하는 정치 단체들은 화요일 중간 선거에 영향을 미치고 AI 규제의 미래를 형성하기 위해 수백만 달러를 소비했습니다. 그 지출은 엇갈린 결과를 가져왔고, 가장 큰 지지를 받은 후보자 중 일부는 경선에서 패했습니다. 업계 측면에서는 선거에 영향을 미치기 위해 돈을 모으고 지출한 두 개의 AI 중심 정치 활동 위원회(PAC)인 American Mission과 Building the Future가 사우스 캐롤라이나 상원 후보 Darline Graham을 지원하기 위해 총 480만 달러를 지출했습니다. American Mission은 공화당의 지출 기관입니다.
articles.content:
Political groups both supporting and opposing the AI industry spent millions of dollars trying to influence Tuesday’s midterm elections and shape the future of AI regulation. That spending produced mixed results, with some of the most heavily backed candidates losing their races.
On the industry side, two AI-focused political action committees (PACs) that raised and spent money to influence the elections — American Mission and Building the Future — collectively spent $4.8 million to back South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost. American Mission is the Republican spending arm of
Leading the Future
(LTF), a broader political group backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz.
American Mission also spent more than $500,000 apiece supporting Republican House candidates Aaron Flint in Montana and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina, both of whom lost. LTF’s Democratic spending arm, Think Big, had better luck backing Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won reelection.
Groups advocating for stronger AI safeguards also saw mixed results.
Public First,
which is backed by Anthropic, supported several Republicans who lost through its affiliated PAC but had more success backing Democratic candidates. It also contributed $3 million to a PAC supporting California state Sen. Scott Wiener, who was leading his race at the time of publication.
Meanwhile,
Guardrails Alliance
, a group that has sought to make taking money from AI companies a political liability, spent more than $1 million apiece opposing two candidates who lost: California Rep. Jimmy Gomez and Montana’s Aaron Flint. It also spent $300,000 supporting Angela Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez.
It’s difficult to separate the impact of AI-related spending from the broader Democratic wave that swept Tuesday’s elections. Elon Musk, who reportedly poured half a billion dollars into supporting Republicans in the midterms, also saw
many of his candidates lose
. Indeed, LTF also backed some candidates it believed were likely to win, only to see them lose to the Dems.
For LTF, though, the general election wasn’t the main focus. The group told TechCrunch ahead of Election Day that it thinks primaries (the contests that choose each party’s nominee) are a more effective use of its money, because spending there can build name recognition and help candidates set up AI policy agendas.
LTF spent $27.38 million in the primaries, including $8 million alone on opposing New York Assembly member
Alex Bores
, who lost his bid for Congress back in June. When deciding whether it’s worth jumping into a general election race, LTF assesses how competitive the race is, whether it thinks spending could make a difference, and whether it should keep its powder dry for future elections.
Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, had a different theory for why LTF spent comparatively little in the general election.
“They don’t want their money to become an issue in these elections,” he said. He pointed to the Michigan Senate primary election, in which a pro-Israel lobbying group called AIPAC spent close to $30 million backing Democratic candidate Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens conceded the primary to El-Sayed, who went on to win the Senate seat.
“AIPAC became the story in that race,” Blaettler said. “We know people hate AI billionaires. They hate the people running these companies. They’re very distrustful and disgusted by the political spending and lobbying that the tech industry does. If they spend in a competitive race, they would just become an enormous liability for their candidates.”
The main fight among AI-related PACs, whether they are pro-industry or pro-regulation, is whether Congress should establish a national AI framework that
overrides state laws
, or whether states will maintain their own ability to impose safeguards.
Neither side seems poised to back down. LTF, which favors a single national AI framework, told TechCrunch it plans to keep spending in the 2028 elections, while Guardrails Alliance says it wants to keep opposing candidates backed by the AI industry.
Blaettler said that while LTF’s ads rarely touch on AI, instead focusing on popular issues for each candidate, Guardrail Alliance’s ads are specifically about who is taking money from the AI industry.
“Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic,” Blaettler said.

articles.title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
articles.title_ko: Uber를 예약하기 위해 AI 에이전트를 사용하는 사람은 거의 없다고 회사는 말합니다.
articles.summary: During its busiest week last quarter, Uber said only four people booked a ride using an AI agent.
articles.summary_ko: 개인 AI 에이전트를 사용하여 Uber를 주문하는 사람은 거의 없습니다. 수요일에 거대 운송업체에 전화를 걸어 회사는 가장 바쁜 주인 10월 할로윈 주 동안 AI 에이전트를 통해 단 4번만 차량 서비스를 주문했다고 밝혔습니다. AI 에이전트를 사용해 배달 서비스인 우버이츠(Uber Eats)를 통해 음식을 주문하는 사람들이 늘었지만, 전체 이동 횟수에 비해 그 양은 여전히 ​​상당히 적었습니다. 월스트리트 분석가들은 이 회사가 할로윈 주간에 Uber와 Uber Eats를 통해 약 3억 2천만 건의 운행과 주문을 처리했지만 Uber Eats 주문은 500건에 불과했다고 말했습니다.
articles.content:
Very few people are using personal AI agents to order Ubers, apparently. On the transportation giant’s
third-quarter earnings
call on Wednesday, the company said that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.
While more people used an AI agent to order food through its delivery service, Uber Eats, the volume was still fairly small compared to the overall number of trips.
Uber’s chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy,
told
Wall Street analysts on the call that the company handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent.
“It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far,” said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, referring to the low number of orders placed by AI agents. “Listen, we hope that there will be more traction.”
The surprisingly low numbers of AI-initiated transactions come amid growing hype for a new wave of AI agents that don’t just answer questions but also handle tasks on users’ behalf. There’s been an explosion of personal AI startups, including one of the buzziest, Instinct, which was founded last year and raised its most recent round of funding at a
$10 billion valuation.
Meta’s Muse also became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users,
per Meta’s own reporting
. The company said many were using it to shop and transact with businesses.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI (Grok) are also now offering their own AI agents, as are
numerous smaller startups.
Still, early numbers from public companies indicate the agentic web still has a long way to go. DoorDash, for instance, said last week on its earnings call that it has
only received a few hundred orders
from AI agents so far, as most customers are still placing orders through the DoorDash app.
Uber is seeing the same behavior, it seems. Khosrowshahi pointed out that the average time to book a ride is only 50 seconds in the company’s app, and re-ordering a favorite food only takes 90 seconds. That suggests an AI agent isn’t necessarily saving anyone time.
Despite the low number of AI-driven transactions, Khosrowshahi seemed bullish on the idea of agents in general. “We think that is another opportunity to reach our platform. We think it will be a net positive in terms of demand on the ecosystem,” he said.
Right now, there are around eight major AI assistants on the market, Khosrowshahi noted, and he expects that number to grow to more than 10 in time.
“Every single AI system company is talking to us,” he added.

articles.title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
articles.title_ko: OpenAI는 이미 2028년 선거를 구체화하려고 노력하고 있습니다.
articles.summary: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane wants AI to define the 2028 election, proposing a new social contract that could benefit Americans while also advancing the AI giant’s own business interests.
articles.summary_ko: OpenAI의 최고 글로벌 업무 책임자인 Chris Lehane은 2028년 대통령 선거가 AI의 결정적인 순간이 될 수 있다고 생각합니다. 그리고 그는 정치인들이 단순히 반 AI 정서에 대해 립서비스를 하는 것이 아니라 기술에 대한 미국인의 우려를 해결하는 정책 개발을 시작하기를 원하며 Lehane은 경제를 재편할 수 있는 AI의 잠재력을 프랭클린 D. 루즈벨트 대통령의 뉴딜(New Deal), 산업화 이후 제정된 1930년대 연방 프로그램 및 개혁 세트와 대공황이 기존 경제 질서를 무너뜨린 것에 비교합니다. 그는 오늘날 미국인들도 비슷한 불안을 느끼고 있다고 관찰합니다.
articles.content:
OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the
backlash against data centers
.
In a
new essay
, Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.
The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from
OpenAI’s policy agenda last year,
which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.
Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.
“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”
While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.
Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.
Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.
Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers.
“I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.”
Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.
Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.
Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and
safeguards around AI companions
for minors. He also warns against keeping
AI out of classrooms
, arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.
Lehane also calls for
enforceable AI safety standards,
independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though
recent studies show
that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.
Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI
opposed
California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also
sought to limit state regulation
, arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent
evaluators embedded
in the company.
Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines.
But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.
Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.
TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

articles.summary: The startup allows software engineers to deploy teams of agents to work on various aspects of a project simultaneously.
articles.summary_ko: , 여러 에이전트를 병렬 작업 공간에 배포하여 사용자가 소프트웨어 프로젝트를 실행할 수 있도록 하는 AI 코딩 스타트업입니다. 수요일에 스타트업의 창립자이자 CEO인 찰리 홀츠(Charlie Holtz)가 말했습니다. 그는 "우리는 다음 인터페이스에 대한 크고 말도 안되는 계획을 가지고 있습니다."라고 덧붙이며 회사가 "내년 초"까지 고객이 사용할 수 있는 "새로운 것"을 갖게 될 것이라고 놀렸습니다. 그는 Meta의 최고 AI 책임자인 Alexandr Wang과 회사 Superintelligence Labs의 제품 책임자인 Nat Friedman과 함께 일하기를 기대하고 있다고 말했습니다. “그들은 절대적인 눈물을 흘리고 있으며 MSL이 가장 높은 인재 밀도를 가지고 있다고 확신합니다…
articles.content:
Meta has acquired
Conductor
, an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.
The news was
originally reported
by Axios, and Conductor
shared news
of its acquisition on its blog.
“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,”
wrote
the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”
On X, Holtz
also noted
that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.
Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.
Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.
Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.
Meta, which previously
lagged behind
in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company
launched Muse Code
, its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company
recently reporting
that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year,
including Moltbook
, the viral agent platform that made headlines.

articles.content:
DuckDuckGo
is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could
turn off Gemini
, but it said shutting off its other AI features would
cost schools Google Search
, as well.
DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are
around 50 million Chromebooks
in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves
over 150 million users
globally.
On X
, DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s
online documentation
, explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.”
Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement,
writing
, “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.”
Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless.
Prove Google wrong.
https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9
— Kamyl Bazbaz (@KamylBazbaz)
November 3, 2026
In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.
The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they
don’t want AI data centers
built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.
Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “
Guided Learning
” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.
After the backlash on Tuesday, Google
defended
its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.
We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced:
– Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control…
— News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle)
November 3, 2026
The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.
DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.
However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website,
noai.duckduckgo.com
, where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.
That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company
reported earlier this year
that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.

Open source models are becoming more mainstream as enterprises, governments and startups alike rely on the promise of lower costs, more control, and more flexibility. Why startups, enterprises, and governments are switching to open AI models to cut costs, and when it makes less sense to use the most powerful models.
Who makes money when the models are free to use, and whether the companies building them can capture the value they create.
Why the U.S. may need deep-pocketed players
like Nvidia
to build an open frontier model that can compete with China’s, and what’s at stake if Chinese models become the global default.
How recent attacks on open AI platforms are raising a difficult question: how do you keep an open ecosystem secure without closing it off?

articles.content:
Google was met with swift backlash on Tuesday after it
announced
that schools using Google’s K-12 software will not be able to use Search unless they opt in to using AI tools.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google,
told
The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a student’s school doesn’t opt in to using AI tools like Gemini, then students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”
Even as Google made this announcement on a busy Election Day, several left-leaning politicians took time to speak up about their concerns.
Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
accused
Google in an X post of “extortion,” writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT)
said on X
that Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.”
President Trump claimed that AI oligarchs could regulate themselves because they “love our country.”
Now, Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.
That’s not love. That’s extortion.
PAUSE AI NOW.
— Sen. Bernie Sanders (@SenSanders)
November 3, 2026
Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair and staunch advocate against monopolies, also condemned Google’s decision as anticompetitive.
“This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” she
wrote
. “Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.”
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of being a monopoly,
commenting
, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”
Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service.
Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains…
https://t.co/eajJN9yfQF
— Lina Khan (@linamkhan)
November 3, 2026
While Search is a necessary tool for information gathering, educators worry that its built-in AI overviews could dissuade students from finding answers themselves. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools,
using a different search engine
isn’t a simple fix.
Google says that it’s working on a “Guided Learning” tool for student accounts in Search, which is supposed to walk students through the process of solving a problem or finding information, rather than just handing them the answer. If a student is struggling with a math problem, for example, the feature may prompt them to refresh their memory about the rules for dividing exponents, instead of spitting out a number.
In response to the backlash, Google pointed out in
a post on X
that it had listened to educators by turning off access to AI products by default and noted that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually.
We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced:
– Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control…
— News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle)
November 3, 2026
“We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google wrote in its statement. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.”

Title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)

URL Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50363461

Markdown Content:
The sole reason LLMs has gotten this good is because their aggressive expansion has been accompanied with literally this. The amount of uncredited information these models have been fed must be astonishing, also terrifying.
I think the heavily subsidized subscriptions are exactly for this purpose - the training data they generate is worth the high subsidy.
i mean openai basically said as much, no? it's free for all so that they can train the models better and get real world interaction data.

Why do you think they’re getting into consulting now? Imagine all those tasty confidential IP and contract documents they have ingested. You couldn’t buy those.
That is, fundamentally the marketing ploy of “AI Safety”. For an AI system to be “completely safe”, like a self-driving car, it must map the full environment it operates in and be taught the “right way” to handle every conceivable scenario. So when you present it with novel data or a situation, that constitutes an “AI safety event”, which per their ToS is a carve out for training on your session. Further, go read the ToS carefully about what you opt out of. You’ll note there’s nary a mention of tool calls. You’re only opting out inputs (what you type) and outputs from the model from being trained on. All the content of the tool calls made while running on your system are fair game for training.
There is no way this is true, no? This'd mean literally all codebases people are working with have been trained on. There's no way anyone would use these guys if that was the case?
Why are you using it if you don’t want it to get better whose data is it supposed to get better on just somebody elses, not yours?
They're supposed to be focused on genuine training improvements over existing data, including via RL. Gathering data under the table is misaligned behavior.
Well for us Europeans, GDPR explicitly allows them to store pretty much anything if somebody can claim it’s for safety. It’s literally just complicating things and providing zero reassurance to us AI customers.

You don’t need user consent to retain data that’s arguably needed to provide the service itself. I guess, safety falls into that category. Training on that data is probably a grey area, if they can guarantee it won’t contain PII. They have stolen all the internet, so I wouldn’t bet highly on their restraint.
I can guarantee you that multiple people are reviewing some chats. This is very similar to Apen and whatever company prior to that for reviewing Google searches. They'd hire out contractors with NDA.
What's worse is if you have a Pixel phone then Gemini is completely useless without enabling this setting. I had it switched off: "Hey Google, remind me at 7pm <something>" "OK, your reminder is set for 7pm" Next day: "Hey Google, why didn't you remind me at 7pm" "I can't do anything with your phone unless you enable chat history." WTAF!

Maps refuses to show your *current* location if you don't enable location accuracy i.e. if you won't allow it to spy on your WiFi or Bluetooth it refuses to show your current location at all. GPS, what's that? We can disable notifications and even phone access but physical activity is the one permission that cannot be disabled for play services !? Google apps have a lot of WTFs!
And the YouTube home page is blank if you have Watch History off. The recommendation algorithm still runs on the side bar of any video you watch, but the home page refuses to even show your subscriptions.
Yeah, this is just Google punishing people for not enabling their data harvesting. There's no reason they can't have a mix of "this is popular in general" and "your subs and likes suggest you'd like this" on the front page - they just don't want people to disable watch history. They are required to offer that as an option, but they'll never stop pestering you about it.
I'm surprised they don't just store your watch history anyway , with the toggle option being "don't show me or people looking over my shoulder my watch history".
My watch history is set to 3 months. It used to constantly show things I had already seen. However eventually (years ago) I just don’t get repeats.

Welcome to monopoly where they get the free videos from the sheep and still order you around. Why has Youtube not been disrupted btw, everyone gave up or did VCs order it?

> And the YouTube home page is blank if you have Watch History off. That one I do like. YouTube’s homepage (at least without an account and with history off) is a cesspool of uninteresting clickbait garbage so I’m glad to have it off. I do agree they seem to think of it as some kind of punishment¹, which makes it all the more satisfying that it works as I want it. ¹ It’s now entirely blank for me, but I remember when they started doing this (it wasn’t always the case) they showed a message that suggested not having a homepage was undesirable.
Agree, but it should at least show recent uploads from my subscription. It's stupid that I can visit "www.youtube.com" and not see a single video.
I have to say - I actually like this. Imagine if you go to Google.com to do a web search, and it is a page full of recommendations on sites to visit. Would you want that?
The difference is that I'm subscribed to a variety of channels on YouTube. Yes, I do want to see their videos on the front page. That's what the Subscriptions page is doing anyway.
Yes, but what algorithm will it use to show videos from the channels you're subscribed to? Will you and everyone else agree with that choice of algorithm? The only one that makes sense is chronological. Anything else leads to similar problems as in the past.

I agree, but most people do not. A quite common complaint of Mastodon - even here on HN - is that chronological makes discovery difficult.
> We can disable notifications and even phone access but physical activity is the one permission that cannot be disabled for play services !? Sandboxed Play Services works on Grapheneos without physical activity so it's definitely not actually required by their services. But I think they showed the best example of that behavior just recently: no AI, no Google search for students because search is "too integrated" with AI ([https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/11/03/google-...](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/11/03/google-will-cut-off-search-engine-access-to-schools-banning-generative-ai/))

People use Google everyday, block all ads, get extremely angry about Google's grubby advertising hands, and then when you tell them their are paid services like Kagi and Proton...."pay for this stuff? Nah, I have a right to it for free!"
Payment doesn't guarantee anything tho. We are right now in a thread about a paid product by Google still spying.

Yes, it's almost like a fairy tale where children are offered candy but then very bad things happen. Hansel und Gretel, etc. We should have known all along!
Continuing with your Hansel and Gretel metaphor, the first time the candy turned sour for me was Goog-411. It was a service (at least over here in the US) that allowed you to look up local businesses via voice prompts over a phone call. When the service was still active, calling 411 via a mobile phone had a per-call cost, so a free lookup service seemed great. I found out later that Goog411 was created to primarily train on the voice prompts from the users of the service. Left a really bad taste.
Surely that approach is implemented to force people in to the _all_ group. Then again, anon YouTube no longer showing recommendations on the start page is what waned me off the website.
I've just turned off location accuracy, google maps displayed a popup said results will be better if I turn it on, and after dismissing the popup it did use GPS to localize me with no issues.

This is the most infuriating part. Complete bait and switch by bricking features of the phone I bought before Gemini for practically anything that used assistant. Anything you link to it to enable basic functionality you had on device before gets them the ability to use it for not just training but ads and measurement.

This has been annoying me too, and I was getting pretty close to turning on chat history having forgotten why I disabled it. Thanks for the reminder OP!

I imagine that will also be part of the context. They are vague when they say 'don't enter'. Is it only prompts or does it also cover other data too.
Wasnt there an announcement some weeks ago here on HN that one of the BigTechs popular services are now including your personal pictures as well? Wasnt it Google?
Your email, Google docs, Google photos, Google home devices etc. are all subject to human review. The data is on their servers. And this goes for all cloud providers btw.
Exactly, I have a Gemini Pro account, I can’t see how privacy can be maintained. If I ask Gemini to take the content of an email and added the dates to my calendar, then all of that private information might as well be public then!
Is this really surprising to anyone? I just sorta assumed that Google was hoovering up anything I type into its AI and don't tell it anything too personal or sensitive. Is anyone under the illusion that our data is not being collected, whether it's Google or literally even the seemingly innocuous TVs in our home that have been found to be spying on us 24/7?

It can be difficult to connect the abstract knowledge that Google collects their data with the concrete reality of an AI training on that data, or a human manually reviewing it.

##  1. Model Introduction

Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model, and our most capable 3T-class model to date. Post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains, it is the first model in the K3.1 series. With a 1-million-token context window, Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers substantial improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, factual accuracy, and other agentic capabilities.

# Introducing Ripple-65B Preview,
a Frontier Open-Weight Model

Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding

Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.

To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.

Today, we release **Ripple-65B Preview**, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, **achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1** and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).

Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.

Ripple-65B Preview is available on [Hugging Face](http://huggingface.co/ricursiveAI/Ripple-65B-Preview), [Together AI](https://www.together.ai/models/ripple-65b-preview), [GMI Cloud](https://console.gmicloud.ai/model/llm/ripple-65b-preview/abfc023e-35b7-4e9e-bb97-cef5db95f171), and [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/ricursiveai/ripple-65b-preview). Fireworks goes live later today.

# Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost

LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs [exceeded $100 million](https://www.wired.com/story/openai-ceo-sam-altman-the-age-of-giant-ai-models-is-already-over/). In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to [$10-100B by 2026 to 2027](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xm6jNMSFT7g&t=805s) for pretraining alone.

In contrast, **we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M,**which is **one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding**, as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.

# Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning

Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.

Our mixed RL recipe uses [truncated importance sampling](https://openreview.net/forum?id=xsonlP8DRV), [score centering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20807), and [linear length penalty](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf) with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved.

The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.

# A Co-Designed Model Architecture

Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.

Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added [FFN activation clipping](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-oss/), [gated attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708), [global NoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18795), and [value residuals](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.17897).

# Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements

We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.

Our starting point was Olmo 3’s[model ladder](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.04403), from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented [StepFun](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.04715v7) batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented [sigmoid gated attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708). Ladder v1.4 (2-stream [mHC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880)) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to [global NoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18795) and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added [value residuals](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.17897). In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.

Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with **16x less compute**. Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.

# Conclusion

We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.

We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.

At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If you’re interested, check out [https://www.ricursive.com/careers](https://www.ricursive.com/careers).

Title: Progress on provable inference for large language models

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference

Published Time: 2026-11-02T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)_

## Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for **provable inference** (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

1.   Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.
    1.   For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.
    2.   Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in [section 6](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#prior-work). Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

2.   Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

*   The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;
*   A [technical report](https://www.anthropic.com/document/flashprove-technical-report) explaining the details of our system;
*   A (Claude-written) [protocol specification](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/paper/paper.pdf) document;
*   [Executable code](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve) that includes: a [prover](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/prover) and two verifiers, a [fast verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/verifier) in C++, and a [provably correct verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/tools/lean-verify) in Lean; and
*   [Lean proofs](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/lean) for the top level mathematical statements, along with an [interactive visualizer](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/lean/STATEMENTS.html) of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.[1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-1) This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

## Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of _provable inference_ (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a _zero-knowledge succinct argument:_ the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short _proof_(say, a few megabytes) that the user can _quickly_ verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals _nothing_ about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an **open-source performant prototype for provable inference**. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in **pacing AI development**, in **providing AI customers with integrity guarantees**, in **facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators**, and more.

## Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises [trust challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07213) that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for _provable inference (PI)._

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (_zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge_). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a _prover_ to convince a _verifier_, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is _zero-knowledge_ in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is _succinct_ in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

### Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to [regulate](https://thefuturesociety.org/international-ai-verification) and [pace](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) AI development rely on [monitoring hardware and how it is used](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08797). For example, a provider might be required to [devote its hardware to inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15867) rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

_How zkSNARKs can help:_ The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.[2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-2) We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

### Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become [prime targets](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html). An attacker or rogue agent may [compromise an inference server](https://www.wiz.io/blog/nvidia-triton-cve-2025-23319-vuln-chain-to-ai-server) to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while [hiding among genuine responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02620). The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of _which weights_ are actually running on its servers? In our [Frontier Safety Roadmap](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap), Anthropic set a [public goal](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap#moonshot-r-d-projects) to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “_We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights._” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.[3](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-3)
