[Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368804) 71 points by [lukeigel](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=lukeigel)[8 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368804) | [hide](https://news.ycombinator.com/hide?id=50368804&goto=item%3Fid%3D50368804) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Launch%20HN%3A%20Kino%20AI%20%28YC%20S23%29%20%E2%80%93%20AI%20media%20manager%20and%20video%20editor&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](https://news.ycombinator.com/fave?id=50368804) | [26 comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368804) Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino ([https://kino.ai](https://kino.ai/)). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at [https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video](https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video) and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at [https://kino.ai/launch-video](https://kino.ai/launch-video) Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052)). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ([https://regressions.net](https://regressions.net/)). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything. The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at [https://kino.ai](https://kino.ai/). We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now. If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you. Would Kino be a great tool or is this best done locally with Claude/Codex? We support very dense MP4 files, ProRes, many different cameras that were filming at the same time, etc. When you sign in there is a workflow button to click on where you just plug in your iPhone, your SD cards, and it will index everything + lay out a quick stringout that makes sense. It helps to also give links to instagram videos whose style you like. Tons of friends are now using us to edit home movies they never would have otherwise, as the footage was just sitting there earlier [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50369844&goto=item%3Fid%3D50368804%2350369844) [krmmalik](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=krmmalik)[6 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50370451) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368804#50369710) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368804#50369212)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Splendid effort and I'm so glad actual industry experts built something like this than someone like me who is just a vibe-coder. Industry experience counts for so much in such cases. One thing I didn't see and I really hope you'll incorporate it is templates. articles.title: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.title_ko: Apple의 Siri Recaps를 사용해 보았습니다. 놀라울 정도로 유용하지만 약간 불안하기도 합니다.
articles.summary: Apple's AI-powered Siri Recaps won me over in just one day, despite my privacy reservations. But there's still room for improvement.
articles.summary_ko: iOS 27.3 및 watchOS 27.3. 베타 버전에는 Apple Watch Series 12 착용자가 중요한 소리를 감지하고, 노래를 식별하고, 대화를 따라잡고, 메모를 작성할 수 있는 4가지 새로운 AI 기능이 포함되어 있습니다. 내 Apple Watch에서 Apple의 Siri Recaps 기능을 사용한 지 하루 만에, AI 기반 오디오 녹음 및 요약에서 나오는 소름 끼치는 요소보다 궁극적으로 그 가치가 어떻게 더 클 수 있는지 이미 알 수 있었습니다. 그러나 AI 지원 메모 작성이 너무 멀리 떨어져서 기억할 가치가 없는 항목을 캡처할 수 있는 부분과 개선의 여지가 있는 부분도 보입니다. 처음 두 개, 소리…
articles.content:
On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of
Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions
of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.
The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.
It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.
Image Credits:
iPhone screenshot by TechCrunch
Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.
Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re
now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
.
I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.
I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.
But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.
I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.
Image Credits:
iPhone screenshot by TechCrunch
For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.
One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.
I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.
Image Credits:
iPhone screenshot by TechCrunch
Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.
This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.
While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.
I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.
I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.
Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.
These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.
Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

Stevie Bonifield

Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in
a post on X
that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced
plans for “AI-native” devices
and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it
won’t
have is a screen:
“Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. Last month, a rumor claimed Nothing is planning to launch
two pairs of AI smart glasses
, including one without cameras, and
an earlier rumor
said it’s “repositioning itself as an AI-first company” with a shift to AI accessories.
Image: Nothing
Nothing’s AI device wouldn’t be the first screen-free AI gadget, following the likes of the
Humane AI pin
, the
Friend
, and even
AI stuffed animals
. OpenAI is also reportedly working on
an AI smart speaker
with Jony Ive. Pei alluded to earlier AI devices, saying, “the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life.” He added, “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end.”

Pei’s description adds up to a screenless non-app that uses AI? He also calls it a “productivity tool.” Adding further mystique to the announcement, Pei seems to downplay any link to AI wearables.

Data centers lost the midterms
In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.﻿
by

Link

Midterm elections 2026: all the news
see all updates
Lauren Feiner
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and
ballot measures
that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry.
Of voters polled by
NBC News
on Election Day, 76 percent
said they opposed data centers
in their communities. Dozens of local communities
voted directly to restrict development
through
ballot measures
. And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development.
It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place.
Ballot measures
Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to
a site compiled by Redbud Consulting
, the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The
Town of Wells, Maine,
favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The
City of El Dorado, Kansas
, voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years.
Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development
Texas
Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a
statewide moratorium on data center development
, while Abbott took a more measured approach. He
announced a new audit
this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has
previously praised
data center expansion in the state.
In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers.
Florida
Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning,
NBC News
reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate.
Pennsylvania
Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro
signed an executive order
that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she
supports a development pause
of up to three years.
Ohio
Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a
leaked memo
that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier
helped install data center tax breaks
as lieutenant governor, though he more recently
introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act
in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone
as far as to call for a moratorium
,
he’s said
that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input.
Republicans warned that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates
Michigan
Democrat and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race over Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was one of the earliest politicians to stake his position on data centers, and
has called
for a pause on new developments “until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers
called for a one-year state moratorium
this summer, but not a federal ban.
As of Wednesday morning,
NBC News
had not yet called a House race between Democratic organizer William Lawrence and Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, but Lawrence held a lead with 92 percent of the vote in. Similar to El-Sayed, Lawrence stated his position on data centers early on, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new developments during his primary campaign. Barrett
introduced legislation
this summer to bar nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and give locals more control.
Maine
Democrat and former Maine State Senator Troy Jackson ousted Republican Sen. Susan Collins from her Senate seat. The state legislature passed what would have been the country’s first moratorium on data centers, had the governor not vetoed it. But polls show that
opposition to data centers
among Maine residents remained strong. Jackson
supported a state moratorium
on data centers, while Collins opposed such a measure but called for more local control and protection for energy ratepayers.
Wisconsin
Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won the governor’s race over Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. Neither Crowley nor Tiffany favored a moratorium on data centers, and have distanced themselves from previous support. Crowley won his primary over progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong, who supported a moratorium.
Both
Crowley and Tiffany said they wanted to end state tax subsidies for data centers though they’ve accused one another of flip-flopping their stances.
Nevada
Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford successfully flipped the governor’s seat from incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo, whom he’d branded “data center Joe.” Lombardo has previously made supportive comments about data centers, but more recently introduced an
executive order
making tax incentives contingent on data centers covering power costs and meeting certain environmental standards. Ford previously championed a 2015 data center tax-break bill, but said today’s data centers are different from those years ago, and now supports a pause on all tax breaks for new data centers.
Georgia
Democrat and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governor’s seat over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Bottoms favored a moratorium on data centers to review environmental and cost effects, while Jackson preferred to leave decisions up to locals.
Arizona
Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs fought off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Both
opposed
a moratorium on data centers in favor of power and water use standards.
Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes held onto her seat over a challenge from Republican state legislator Warren Petersen. Mayes took a more hardline view than her Democratic peer, Hobbs, by endorsing a state moratorium on data center development. Petersen
opposed a moratorium
, and said data centers are necessary for technology residents use every day.
Iowa
Democratic state auditor Rob Sand won the governor’s seat over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand did not support a data center moratorium, which Lahn did. But both agreed on ending tax breaks for the developments.
South Carolina
Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina’s Senate seat blue in a race against Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who had taken over the seat after her brother Lindsey Graham died. Andrews supported a two-year data center moratorium, while Graham opposed a pause and
got significant support
from a super PAC allied with the data center industry.

# The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell

## AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt

02 Nov 2026

4 min read

 3

Dina Genkina is the computing and hardware editor at IEEE Spectrum

 iStock

[cybersecurity](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/cybersecurity)[internet](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/internet)[artificial intelligence](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/artificial-intelligence)

In late October, a [slew](https://www.wiz.io/blog/cve-2026-111497-brotli-rce-node-js) of [major](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/ruby-fixes-three-regex-engine-bugs.html)[cybersecurity](https://scotthelme.co.uk/eight-bits-of-trust-emudhras-ca-keys-cracked-in-milliseconds/) issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called [PHP2Shell vulnerability](https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/#what-we-need-from-you), which put a plethora of websites, including those of [NASA](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/nasa), [Wikipedia](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/wikipedia), the White House, and all other sites that run on [Wordpress](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/wordpress) or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.

As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by [cybersecurity](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-cybersecurity-mythos) researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.

“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says [Matt Suiche](https://www.linkedin.com/in/msuiche/), AI security research lead at the [cybersecurity](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/cybersecurity) startup [Tolmo](https://tolmo.com/). “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”

## PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors

PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was [reported](https://calif.io/php2shell/) to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.

“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says [Suman Jana](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~suman/), an associate professor of computer science at [Columbia University](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/columbia-university).

“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” **–Suman Jana, Columbia University**

Title: ‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?

URL Source: https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/what-can-save-the-british-high-street-rotherham

Published Time: 2026-11-04T15:18:46.000Z

Markdown Content:
O n 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.

Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.

The big-box alternative … Rotherham’s Parkgate retail park.

Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost [half of Britons don’t visit their high street](https://www.ipsos.com/en-uk/ipsos-reveals-high-prices-and-declining-high-streets-key-local-concerns-britons) weekly. Instead, shoppers are [opting for retail parks](https://brc.org.uk/news-and-events/news/corporate-affairs/2025/ungated/retail-parks-lead-the-way-as-footfall-sees-small-bounce-in-february/). Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even [paying extra](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2026/07/03/british-retailers-are-running-out-of-space/) to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, [sit at 13%](https://www.savills.co.uk/research_articles/229130/390116-0), reports Savills.

Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”

Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.

A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, [are vacant](https://moderngov.rotherham.gov.uk/mgConvert2PDF.aspx?ID=159086), far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.

‘It’s either here or Meadowhall’ … Jo and Richard Hill at Parkgate, Rotherham.

The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would [drain jobs](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written-answers/1987/jul/24/retail-developments-1?utm-source=chatgpt.com) from the high street, “[disembowel towns and villages](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1994/may/10/approval-of-certain-markets-no-3)” and disadvantage those [unable to drive](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1990/jun/08/jones-brothers-islington).

Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.

The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a [government analysis](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67cf14549e1670eb1afaa661/_WITHDRAWN_Rotherham.pdf) found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. [Recent police data](https://www.southyorkshire.police.uk/area/your-area/south-yorkshire/rotherham/rotherham-central/about-us/crime-map) shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre [recorded 836 crimes](https://www.southyorkshire.police.uk/area/your-area/south-yorkshire/sheffield/sheffield-city-centre/about-us/crime-map) in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”

For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.

Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.

Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”

‘I’ve seen a massive change’ … Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer in Rotherham town centre.

The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: [research by the thinktank Power to Change](https://www.powertochange.org.uk/evidence-and-ideas/research-and-reports/introducing-the-shuttered-front-revisiting-the-high-street-warning-lights/) published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”

* * *

T he town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.

Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?

She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.

‘Recently, people are just careful with money’ … Dannii Paston outside her shop, Yella Brick Road.

The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.

London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. Apple is reportedly cutting budgets for its internal AI usage
Apple is cutting the daily amount its engineering teams can spend on AI, Bloomberg
reported
Wednesday. It’s a big change for a company that has worked
to integrate
the technology into its engineering processes.
In October, Apple lowered the daily AI spending cap for its engineering teams, decreasing it from $300 to $200, the outlet reported. And more cuts are in the works, with some allowances falling to $100 a day, sources tell Bloomberg. Outside engineering, Apple is reportedly weighing a daily limit as low as $25 a day.
TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for comment.
Earlier this year, a
tsunami of tokenmaxxing
took hold, with companies pushing staff to use AI as much as possible in the name of vaguely defined efficiency gains. The frenzy was short-lived, however, as bills for said tokens came due, and companies decided that token rationing might be a more fiscally sensible approach.
Concerns persist
about an apparent gap between what AI costs to build and run and the (often unclear) productivity gains the technology is suppose to generate.

Victoria Song
is a senior reporter and author of the
Optimizer
newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine.
This is
Optimizer
, a weekly newsletter sent from
Verge
senior reviewer
Victoria Song
that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for
Optimizer
here
.
“How does that make you feel?”
I get asked this a lot in therapy. Plenty of life events, big and small, have triggered this question. Three weeks ago, it was the fact that I had to ask my therapist for her consent because I was wearing the
Amazon Bee Frontier
during our session.
That first week, I didn’t really have an answer. A lot had changed since I first tested
Bee
, an always-recording AI wearable, early last year. The elevator pitch is that it listens to all your conversations and uses AI to transcribe and summarize them. From there, it has a List feature that suggests to-dos, a Grow feature for identifying areas where you can improve, and various summaries that analyze the content, tone, and takeaways from your conversations. It’s even got a chatbot that can answer questions about yourself or what was said and when.
In the last 19 months, it’s gotten better at distinguishing my actual speech from TV dialogue. It can now pull in information from my calendar and photos app, and suggest things to buy on Amazon based on what I’ve said. At times, particularly for job-related tasks, it’s helped me remember talking points. But most of the time, it’s led to me questioning my reality.
My therapist usually lets me arrive at my own decisions, even if I often take the scenic route to the obvious conclusion. After 11 years, she’s intimately acquainted with the wackier parts of my job. But in my third week of talking about Bee, my therapist requested that I chuck this thing right out a window.
It’s easy to forget this thing is recording when you’re just going about your day.
It’s a bit dark, but a big reason I’m in therapy is to build trust in my own memories. I grew up with
a dad who might’ve been a spy
and an immigrant family that never agreed on a single version of events. Growing up, I felt unmoored. Were things truly as I’d remembered them? Were my parents the unreliable narrators, or was I? Adding in their eventual dementia to the mix made discerning truth from fiction even harder.
In those moments, I had wished for a device like Bee. A reviewable record, so to speak, for moments where I wanted a sanity check. It’s funny in retrospect. Now that tech companies have started making this fantasy into a reality, what I
feel
is perpetually gaslit.
For example, it’s disorienting to see Bee’s transcripts and summaries of my conversations, often because the AI remembers and interprets them differently than I do. Like any AI, it’s not always precise about who said what. In the past three weeks, it’s concluded that I argue with a coworker’s spouse frequently (I’ve never met them), that I think a family member has undiagnosed bipolar disorder (No one
ever
said that!), and that I like to put my good pants on for important video calls. (That was a joke.) Sure, it’s a relief that Bee’s newly updated transcription prowess was able to discern that I personally was not working with detectives Rust Cohle and Marty Hart to find a serial killer named the Yellow King simply because I watched
True Detective
. But it still doesn’t know how to handle the fact that we call my two cats Petey and Pablo various nicknames. By Bee’s estimation, I have about six additional cats named Mr. Handsome, Mr. Stylish, District Attorney Hoss, Dabah Doo Bah, Potato Demon, and Tubby McTubberson Jones.

This was a joke.
These mistakes are at least funny. It’s when the conversations are serious that I feel the strongest whiplash. That’s when the “improved” AI dislodges something in my brain.
In my second therapy session with Bee recording, I spent the majority of the time unpacking my feelings about
You Can See Everything
. It’s a reality-bending movie that questions the line between truth and fiction. As much as I enjoyed the film, witnessing compulsive liars for three hours was bound to take me back to unhappier moments in my life. I should’ve turned Bee off for this session. But the truth is, I just
forgot
. Because the design of these devices is, in many ways, built for you to forget they’re listening.
One of Bee’s capabilities is that it learns “facts” about you that you then swipe right to approve as true, or left to dismiss as false. After this session, it generated a “fact” about an instance of domestic violence I experienced as a child. This particular moment has come up multiple times in sessions over the years — revisiting it has been key to understanding and forgiving my parents, holding compassion for the circumstances that shaped them.
I did not expect how awful it felt to see a traumatic event summarized so starkly in plain English. I hated having to swipe right to say, “Yes, this is true.” I didn’t expect the accompanying summary to be titled “Reclaiming Reality from Manipulative Power.” Or for it to characterize the type of person I am (deeply unsettled), the timbre of the conversation (intense, reflective, emotionally raw), or how I felt during that session (grieving, angry, and clear-eyed about manipulation).
I
remember that session as cathartic. There were times when I laughed or joked around. The topic was serious, yes, but I wasn’t ranting, raving, or crying. I left that session feeling light — you’d never guess that from the summary. Looking at it weeks later, I’m now wondering who’s right: me, or the AI.
This device is, at times, extremely weird.
I also forgot to turn Bee off during my annual physical. I was late to the appointment, and when I changed into a gown for the exam, the damn thing was just sitting in a pile of my clothes. I only realized my mistake when it was time to leave.
On the one hand, it did memorialize that my doctor prescribed me Claritin for allergies and that the nurse and I talked about my dead dog Daisy. (It described me as wistful and grieving here, too, but
I
recall it as fond remembrance.) Ironically, it also memorialized my
doctor
’s feelings on AI transcription. My doctor’s AI transcription software requires patient consent and helps her with long conversations where she has to remember treatment notes. But it’s also garbage at distinguishing between two female speakers, and she spends a decent amount of time correcting it.
Depending on which Bee AI template I use, it can change the summary. With the default template, the AI’s conclusions about this particular meeting include tonal analysis and takeaways. If I filter to the medical visit template, suddenly everything is much more factual. It strips away the ruminations. It’s more useful and less uncomfortable to look back on. But I also can’t help but feel that the record of what was a fairly significant healthcare appointment differs from my memory. Who is right?
So, how
does
this all make me feel?
A little bit crazy and overwhelmed. Sometimes offended. Bee has a new-ish feature called Grow. Based on your conversation history, it compiles recommendations on how you can grow as a person. It also generates suggested to-dos.
To train Bee AI on my voice, during setup it asked me to describe my hobbies. I said I enjoy reading, calligraphy, cross-stitch, and running. I’ve recently gotten into fountain pens and ink swatching for journaling. You have to talk for about two minutes straight, so I ended up rambling about how I was unsure whether embroidery would be a natural progression from cross-stitch or an unnecessary side quest at this point in time.
The Grow insight based on this incredibly unserious, one-sided discussion? A conversation Bee itself prompted. I dabble in too many hobbies without serious commitment. A jack of all trades, master of none. I’ve shown no progression or tangible sign of “shareable output” and should spend the next three months picking
one
hobby. Because I allowed Bee to integrate with my reminders list, which has an old to-read list for books I want physical copies of, it confidently stated that despite calling myself a reader, I haven’t made much progress this year.
I don’t recall asking for judgement about my “serial pattern of experimentation.”
Bitch
, I thought, I’ve finished 39 books in 2026 so far. I’ve been practicing calligraphy and journaling for
17 years
. I finished 10 cross-stitch projects this year. Most importantly, hobbies aren’t something I do for “shareable output.” I happen to firmly believe that hobbies should be exempt from cockamamie Silicon Valley-brained KPIs.
Another Grow insight from some political discussion with my spouse about the midterms? “These frameworks help her contextualize current events but may also distance her from present-tense engagement; her tone in political discussion is more analytical than activist, more diagnostic than mobilized.” It then suggested that I “identify one concrete political action aligned with your values that requires less than 30 minutes and complete it this week.”
In
my
memory, this was because we watched an episode of
The Daily Show
and I said, jokingly, that I was tired of US political shenanigans. Never mind my
actual
lived experience canvassing and as a union organizer and representative.
These are just two examples. Imagine seeing some version of this every day for nearly a month. Summaries that are maybe 75 percent right, 15 percent taken out of context, and 10 percent out-of-pocket wrong. Things that are just presented to you as fact, regardless of whatever disclaimer that AI can make mistakes.
You can know the truth deep in your gut and still wonder what happens when your hypervigilance slips.
I said as much in my third therapy session wearing Bee. I asked my therapist to weigh in. What, I joked, did she feel watching me go through this experiment?
I’ve gone through the Bee transcript of that conversation. Ironically, it didn’t summarize her thoughts on how poorly designed this device is for anxious people. I had to dig into the raw transcript to find that. According to my therapist, a device like this likely supersedes a person’s ability to trust their own instincts about what they need to do. When you outsource that, AI can generate insights that aren’t emotionally attuned and, in turn, exacerbate many of the problems a person might be trying to solve. For me, it likely triggers rumination, spiraling, and perfectionism.
That’s the point where we joked that I should probably throw this thing out the window. We laughed that we’d
both
feel relieved when I’m not wearing this at my next session. I would say that was the most important takeaway.
Bee didn’t include that in my suggested to-do list. It did, however, say this: buy nail glue, complete with a link out to
Amazon.
